evidence.inferred: A 12-inch-style song form: verse and chorus with Moulton's break added and the intro and outro extended for DJs; 112 bars at 120 BPM is 3.7 min, the 7-inch length of 'I Feel Love' (3:46); an extended mix repeats the break and choruses toward the 12-inch's 8:16.

lineages.name: Earl Young
lineages.why: The MFSB drummer at Sigma Sound for Gamble and Huff, whose drumming drove Harold Melvin & the Blue Notes' 'The Love I Lost' and who is credited with the four-on-the-floor disco beat. He cut everything at 120 BPM so DJs could mix it and used crisp open and closed hi-hats they could hear while cueing; he founded and led the Trammps.

lineages.name: Tom Moulton
lineages.why: Extended records for DJs, nearly doubling Don Downing's 'Dream World' in 1974 and introducing what became the disco break. He pioneered the 12-inch single and made the first continuous-mix album side, for Gloria Gaynor.

lineages.name: Giorgio Moroder
lineages.why: At Musicland in Munich he wrote the 'I Feel Love' bassline first and had it played by a Moog modular synchronised to tape via a reference pulse, recorded in 20-30 second bursts because the Moog drifted out of tune. Only the kick was played by a person; the track dropped disco's orchestra entirely.

lineages.name: Nile Rodgers and Bernard Edwards (Chic)
lineages.why: Edwards said his basslines were usually a reaction to Rodgers' guitar rhythms and that the two were a rhythm section even without drums; 'Le Freak' grew from a jam after they were turned away from Studio 54 on New Year's Eve 1977. Their records made soulful use of major, minor and extended minor seventh chords.

name: Disco

notes.text: Earl Young's beat: four kick drums a measure, snare on 2 and 4, an eighth-note hi-hat on top, opened with a hiss on the off-beat; he used the hi-hat so DJs could hear it in their headphones when cueing.
Tempos were set for mixing: Young cut everything at 120 so DJs could mix his records into anything; measured disco sits 119-124 BPM in its middle half.

Songs with verses and choruses, extended for clubs: Tom Moulton lengthened records for DJs, invented the break (breakdown) and the 12-inch single, and made the first continuous-mix album side for Gloria Gaynor.
Harmony ranges from two-chord vamps to full cycles of fifths; major and minor sevenths are its staple colour, with extended minor guitar chords (m9, m11) from Rodgers and Edwards.

Syncopated lines in broken octaves (the octave notes sounded one after the other); Bernard Edwards outlined chord tones and used 16th-note anticipations into the next bar, with the major-sixth to minor-seventh move over the IV.
Moroder's sequenced alternative: the 'I Feel Love' bassline was composed first on a Moog modular locked to tape, each note doubled by a delay panned opposite for a strobing pulse.
Orchestral: strings and horns over electric pianos (Rhodes, Wurlitzer), Clavinet and chicken-scratch rhythm guitar; productions used large ensembles and up to 64 tracks.
Bernard Edwards avoided a pick but played as if holding one, thumb and forefinger, striking the string with the top and bottom of the finger — a picked attack from the fingers.
The 12-inch format let mastering engineers cut louder, with wider dynamic range and more bass than a 7-inch — disco's loudness came from the groove width, not a limiter.
Hooks can be tiny: the 'Good Times' chorus melody spans two semitones (A4-B4), fully diatonic and stepwise, carried by rhythm over the vamp.
Guitar and bass lock as their own rhythm section: Edwards' basslines were reactions to Rodgers' guitar rhythms, and he considered the pair a rhythm section even without drums.
The singer and the dancefloor are the subject; the genre came out of Black and gay underground clubs, and 'Disco Inferno' marked its move into the mainstream.

pitfalls.text: Programming it like house: disco's drums were played by people like Earl Young, with the open hi-hat opening and closing on the off-beat; the four-on-the-floor alone is not disco.
Triad-only chords: disco's colour is in major and minor sevenths and extended minor chords; use them even over a two-chord vamp.
A bassline that sits on the roots: syncopate it, break the octaves, and answer the guitar the way Edwards reacted to Rodgers.

progressions.text: 'Good Times': Em7 to A7(sus4) — a ii-V shape that never resolves because E is home, E Dorian.

progressions.roman: i - iv7 - VII7 - IIImaj7 - VImaj7 - ii - V7
progressions.text: 'I Will Survive': the complete minor circle of fifths, ii half-diminished and a harmonic-minor V7 turning back to i, repeated through the song.
MusicRadar's disco seventh-chord loop (Cm7, Abmaj7, Gm7 in C minor): minor and major sevenths over a metronomic 4/4.

evidence.inferred: Broken-octave eighth-note lines (Wikipedia) give 8 a bar; Bernard Edwards' 'Good Times' mixes on-beat hits, straight eighths and 16th anticipations with gaps (TalkingBass), about 6-10; Moroder's 'I Feel Love' line is every note doubled by a delay, reaching 16th-note density.
Counted from the cited analyses: 'Good Times' is a two-chord vamp (Em7, A7) and 'I Will Survive' a full minor circle of fifths of eight chords (Am, Dm7, G7, Cmaj7, Fmaj7, Bm7b5, E7sus4, E7).

Both cited progressions move almost entirely by fourth or fifth — 'Good Times' Em7 to A7 and back, 'I Will Survive' descending the circle of fifths — while MusicRadar's Cm7-Abmaj7-Gm7 loop moves by thirds and seconds; half is the floor.
'Good Times' is fully diatonic to E Dorian (1.0); 'I Will Survive' stays in A minor except the harmonic-minor E7 (7 of 8 chords, 0.875).

Disco was released in two lengths: 'I Feel Love' runs 3:46 on the 7-inch, 5:56 on the album and 8:16 on the 12-inch; Moulton's extended mixes nearly doubled a single's length. Side-long versions (15-17 min) are the outliers.

references.listenFor: Earl Young's own band: the four-on-the-floor kick, 2-and-4 snare and hissing off-beat hi-hat as he invented them.
references.title: Disco Inferno

references.listenFor: The Moog bassline doubled by a delay (dry left, echo right) over a played kick and off-beat hat; compare the 3:46, 5:56 and 8:16 versions.
references.title: I Feel Love

references.listenFor: The complete minor-key circle of fifths in A minor at 116 BPM, cycling under the whole song.
references.title: I Will Survive

references.listenFor: The Em7-A7 Dorian vamp at 110 BPM and Edwards' bass: on-beat hits, eighth-note climbs, and 16th anticipations into bars 2, 3 and 4.
references.title: Good Times

summary: 1970s dance music on a played four-on-the-floor beat — a kick on every beat, snare on 2 and 4, and eighth- or sixteenth-note hi-hats that open with a hiss on the off-beat — at roughly 115-126 BPM. Over it sit syncopated, often broken-octave basslines, chicken-scratch rhythm guitar, electric pianos, and string and horn sections. The 12-inch single and the extended mix with its break, and Moroder's sequenced synthesizers, turned it into the template house and techno grew from.
